title: Excerpta Controversiae
author: Seneca the Elder

passages.original: OVIDIVS NASO aput Arellium Fuscum magistrum suum hanc controuersiam declamauit; nam Latronis admirator erat. Latro in praefatione quadam dixit: non uides ut immota fax torpeat et ignes exagitata restituat? mollit uiros otium, ferrum situ rubiginem ducit. Naso dixit: uidi ego iactatas mota face crescere flammas et rursus nullo concutiente mori. hic autem dixit: quicquid laboris est in hoc est, ut uxori uirum et uxorem uiro diligere concedas. necesse est deinde ut iurare permittas, si amare permiseris.
passages.english: Ovidius Naso declaimed this controversia at the school of Arellius Fuscus, his teacher; for he was an admirer of Latro. Latro said in a certain preface: "Do you not see how a torch left unmoved grows sluggish, and when shaken restores its fires? Leisure softens men; iron, through neglect, gathers rust." Naso said: "I have seen flames grow when tossed by a moving torch, and die again when no one shook it." He also said this: "All the difficulty lies in this, that you allow the husband to love the wife and the wife to love the husband. It follows then that you must permit them to swear, if you have permitted them to love."
passages.notes: Ovid's line about the torch is verse (cf. Amores 1.2.11–12).

passages.original: ALFIVS FLAVVS hanc sententiam dixit: ipse sui et alimentum erat et damnum. Hunc CESTIVS quasi corrupte dixisset obiurgans: apparet, inquid, te poetas studiose legere: iste sensus eius est qui hoc saeculum amatoriis non artibus tantum sed sententiis impleuit. Ouidius enim in libris metamorfoseon dicit: ipse suos artus lacero diuellere morsu coepit et infelix minuendo corpus alebat.
passages.english: Alfius Flavus delivered this epigram: "He was himself both his own nourishment and his own loss." Cestius, rebuking him as though he had spoken in a corrupt style, said: "It is evident that you read the poets eagerly: that idea belongs to the man who has filled this age not only with arts of love but with epigrams. For Ovid in the books of the Metamorphoses says: 'He began himself to tear his limbs apart with mangling bite, and, unhappy, fed his body by diminishing it.'"

passages.original: quaedam enim scolae iam quasi obscena refugiunt nec si qua sordidiora sunt aut ex cotidiano usu repetita possunt pati. Ille in hoc scolasticis morem gerebat, ne uerbis calcatis et obsoletis uteretur; sed quaedam antiqua et a Cicerone dicta, a ceteris deinde deserta dicebat, quae ne ille quidem orationis citatissimae cursus poterat abscondere. adeo quicquid insolitum est etiam in turba notabile est.
passages.english: For certain schools now shrink from some words as if obscene, and cannot bear any that are rather low or drawn from everyday use. He humoured the schoolmen in this, that he did not use trite and worn-out words; but he did use certain old words, spoken by Cicero and then abandoned by the rest, which not even the rush of his very rapid speech could hide. So true is it that whatever is unusual is noticeable even in a crowd.

passages.original: Non postulo ut gloriosum mori, sed ut tutum sit. Non magis crudeles sunt qui uolentes uiuere occidunt, quam qui uolentes mori non sinunt. Curtius deiciendo se in praecipitem locum fatum sepulturae miscuit; celebretur Cato: huic miserrimo, quod aliquid non ignaue de spiritu suo statuit, tantum inpune sit. Etiam uulnera infelicis in crimen scrutantur. Aestimate an uiuere licuerit, cui ne mori quidem licuit. Pars altera.
passages.english: I do not demand that dying be glorious, but that it be safe. Those who kill people who wish to live are no more cruel than those who do not allow people who wish to die [to do so]. Curtius, by hurling himself into a chasm, combined his death with his burial; let Cato be celebrated: for this most wretched man, because he made a not cowardly decision about his own life, let him at least go unpunished. Even the wounds of the unhappy man are searched for grounds of accusation. Judge whether he was permitted to live, who was not even permitted to die. The other side.

passages.original: Multa oratores, historici, poetae Romani a Graecis dicta non subripuerunt, sed prouocauerunt. Thvucydidis sententia est: deinai\ ga\r ai( eu)praci/ai sugkru/yai kai\ suskia/sai ta\ e(ka/stwn a(marth/mata. Sallusti: res secundae mire sunt uitiis obtentui. Cum sit praecipua in Thucydide uirtus breuitas, hac eum Sallustius uicit, et in suis illum castris cecidit. nam in sententia Graeca tam breui habes quae saluo sensu detrahas: deme uel sugkru/yai, uel suskia/sai, uel e(ka/stwn, constabit sensus, etiamsi non aeque comptus, aeque tamen integer.
passages.english: Many things said by the Greeks Roman orators, historians and poets did not steal but challenged. Thucydides' epigram is: "For good fortune is clever at hiding and overshadowing each man's faults." Sallust's: "Prosperity is a wonderful screen for vices." Although brevity is the chief virtue in Thucydides, Sallust surpassed him in it and defeated him in his own camp. For in the Greek epigram, short as it is, you have words you could remove without harm to the sense: take away either sunkrupsai ["to hide"], or suskiasai ["to overshadow"], or hekastōn ["of each"], and the sense will stand, if not equally polished, yet equally complete.
passages.notes: Greek given in Beta Code in the source.

passages.original: at ex Sallustii sententia nihil demi sine detrimento sensus potest. T. autem Liuius tam iniquus Sallustio fuit, ut hanc ipsam sententiam et tamquam translatam et tamquam corruptam dum transfertur obiceret Sallustio: nec amore Thucydidis facit, ut illum praeferat, sed laudat quem non timet et facilius putat posse a se Sallustium uinci, si ante a Thucydide uincatur.
passages.english: But from Sallust's epigram nothing can be removed without damage to the sense. Titus Livy, however, was so unfair to Sallust that he reproached him with this very epigram, as both translated and corrupted in the translating; and he does not do it from love of Thucydides, so as to prefer him, but he praises one he does not fear, and thinks Sallust can more easily be beaten by himself if he is first beaten by Thucydides.
